routes.description: Present objective moral facts and duties, moral knowledge, moral transformation, and moral rationality as a connected body of evidence, then compare classical theism with secular ethical accounts under abductive explanatory criteria.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the four moral phenomena warrant explanation, classical theism is a legitimate explanatory candidate, and its account of their authority, accessibility, transformative horizon, and relation to fulfillment provides qualified comparative support for theism.

motionBridge.description: Comparative explanation of the four moral phenomena must provide at least a qualified increase in the plausibility of classical theism within a cumulative case.

centralBridges.description: Objective value and categorical obligation, moral knowledge, moral transformation, and morality’s rational relation to fulfillment must be established as genuine explananda.
A morally perfect, omniscient, and omnipotent creator must qualify as a coherent candidate capable of explaining the identified moral phenomena.
The theistic account must explain the authority and breadth of moral experience better than naturalistic, cultural, instrumental, or axiomatic alternatives.
The comparative advantage must remain evidentially relevant after accounting for prior plausibility, an incomplete candidate pool, combined alternatives, and the argument’s cumulative role.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Moral phenomenology and properly basic moral apprehension must support irreducible categorical authority rather than merely chosen goals or social conditioning.
Theism must offer resources for complete moral transformation and for harmony between moral life and ultimate human fulfillment.

routes.description: Challenge both the proposed moral explananda and the admission of God into the explanatory comparison while showing how well-being, empathy, culture, natural processes, and disciplined inquiry can account for moral judgment and change.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if theism lacks demonstrated candidacy or comparative explanatory advantage, or if secular accounts adequately accommodate the four moral phenomena while theistic grounding leaves additional epistemic, methodological, or hiddenness problems.

motionBridge.description: The four moral phenomena must fail to provide a warranted comparative inference from moral experience to classical theism.

centralBridges.description: God’s eligibility and the adequacy of the explanatory candidate pool must be justified before comparative abduction can support a theistic conclusion.
Well-being, empathy, shared physical needs, learning, culture, and natural processes must adequately explain moral evaluation, conscience, knowledge, and ordinary transformation.
Objective means-end assessment after adopting foundational values must remain viable without an additional divine source of categorical obligation.
Problems of divine identification, access to divine requirements, unconstrained supernatural hypotheses, and hiddenness must defeat the claimed theistic advantage.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Variation in guilt and moral intuition must support cultural and psychological explanations rather than an inference to universally apprehended divine authority.
Any comparative conclusion must be constrained by priors, bad-lot concerns, combined secular alternatives, and the limited reach of moral intuition.

sections.title: Abductive Method, Candidate Pool, and Conclusion
sections.rationale: This issue governs whether classical theism may enter the explanatory comparison, how candidate-pool and prior-plausibility constraints apply, and what qualified conclusion comparative success could support.

sections.title: Objective Moral Facts and Categorical Authority
sections.rationale: The principal ontological clash concerns whether binding moral obligations are irreducibly categorical and call for a personal moral ground, or can be understood through foundational values and objective relations to well-being.

sections.title: Moral Knowledge, Guilt, and Conscience
sections.rationale: This issue tests whether moral axioms, guilt, and apparent authority disclose genuine moral truths requiring theistic explanation or arise adequately through empathy, culture, learning, and shared human conditions.

sections.title: Moral Transformation and Its Horizon
sections.rationale: Transformation is an express part of the motion, requiring comparison between theistic hope for complete moral formation and secular mechanisms that produce behavioral and character change.

sections.title: Moral Rationality, Flourishing, and Scope
sections.rationale: This issue examines whether morality is rationally congruent with ultimate fulfillment and whether flourishing-based accounts can cover categorical duties, animal suffering, character, and apparent conflicts between morality and self-interest.

sections.title: Comparative Worldview Fit and Theistic Liabilities
sections.rationale: The final comparison integrates explanatory breadth with challenges involving divine identification, access, methodological restraint, hiddenness, naturalistic reduction, and the cumulative evidential role claimed for morality.

moves.speaker: David Baggett
moves.proposition: Theism and secular ethical theories should be compared by standard explanatory criteria for their accounts of moral facts, knowledge, transformation, and rationality.
moves.attributionBasis: David explicitly introduces his own abductive moral argument and develops its phenomena, candidates, criteria, and limited conclusion without a speaker change.

response.rationale: The move constructively establishes the comparative abductive method, identifies four classes of moral phenomena, and proposes explanatory criteria and rival candidates.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it clearly establishes the debate's governing method and the phenomena to be compared.

precisionFindings.rationale: The comparative proposal, its four explananda, and its limited evidential purpose are recoverable and consistently framed.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The framework proposes comparative support rather than deduction and expressly limits the intended conclusion.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The method coherently links explanatory criteria, rival candidates, and a qualified comparative conclusion, with only the explananda premise compressed.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move identifies relevant phenomena and standard criteria, but largely asserts that each phenomenon needs the proposed kind of explanation.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supplies the motion-level comparative framework on which the entire affirmative route depends.

representationalCharity.rationale: This constructive methodological proposal does not materially characterize a live opposing argument.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt expressly names moral knowledge, transformation, rationality, phenomena needing explanation, and both theistic and secular candidates.

moves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
moves.proposition: The abductive case has not justified either that the asserted moral phenomena require further explanation or that God qualifies as a reasonable candidate explanation.
moves.attributionBasis: David directly passes the discussion to Matt, and this sustained first-person response is identifiable as Matt's opening critique until David resumes.

components.text: The framework must justify that the asserted moral phenomena require further explanation and that God belongs in the candidate pool.

response.rationale: The reply expressly diagnoses two prerequisites left unsupported by the framework—explanandum status and divine candidacy—and states that comparison cannot yet warrant theism.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It directly challenges the framework's decisive entry conditions, though its own defense of the exclusion standard remains compressed.

precisionFindings.rationale: The two objections and their conditional relation to the proposed abductive inference are explicitly distinguishable.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The lack-of-justification claim is source-grounded, though the move moves quickly from absence in the presentation to inadequacy.

charity.alternative: The framework offers comparative rather than deductive support and may treat God as one hypothesis to be assessed rather than presupposed.
charity.decisiveQualification: Even a comparative proposal needs some account of why the phenomena are explananda and why the candidate is sufficiently specified to compare.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The two threshold objections coherently undercut the inference, although the standard for admitting explanatory candidates is not fully developed.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The excerpt specifically identifies the missing candidacy justification, but offers limited positive support for excluding God or denying further explanation.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks whether the motion-level comparative inference may begin or support its proposed conclusion.

representationalCharity.rationale: The objection preserves the framework's abductive character while pressing its genuine threshold requirements.

moves.evidenceBasis: The source conditionally grants objective moral phenomena, then asks what candidates qualify and says no justification has been shown for positing God.

moves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
moves.proposition: Moral transformation can occur through secular natural processes, and even a false belief in divine supervision could motivate behavioral improvement.
moves.attributionBasis: Matt explicitly isolates moral transformation as one component of David's case and develops a sustained counterexplanation in his own turn.

components.text: The claimed need for a distinctively theistic explanation of moral transformation requires comparison with secular mechanisms.

response.rationale: The reply contacts the framework's transformation explanandum by offering natural processes and separating behavioral efficacy of belief from the truth of that belief.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the decisive comparative issue but addresses ordinary improvement rather than the later, stronger total-transformation horizon.

precisionFindings.rationale: The secular-process and false-belief points are clear, but moral transformation shifts toward behavioral improvement without a stable depth condition.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speaker uses 'so far as we can tell,' but the evidential basis for a fully natural explanation remains thin.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinction between causal efficacy and truth is sound, but ordinary behavioral improvement does not cover every plausible sense of transformation.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The false-belief example supports the causal point, while the broader naturalistic explanation is asserted without representative mechanisms or comparison.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It materially supports the central secular-account bridge by addressing one of the motion's four express phenomena.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move advances a rival explanation without a sufficiently developed opposing alternative to test for caricature.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt says change can occur through secular material means and notes that a false belief can still motivate a good action.

moves.speaker: David Baggett
moves.proposition: Comparative explanatory superiority cannot overcome a sufficiently low intrinsic probability, so the moral evidence supplies at most a qualified reason for theism within the total evidence.
moves.attributionBasis: David resumes after Matt and the moderator, explicitly addressing the ambition objection; Matt's brief clarification is incorporated into David's completed answer.

components.text: The objection demands a conclusion proportioned to candidate uncertainty, prior plausibility, and the limited comparative evidence.
A secular explanation of one phenomenon limits the breadth and force of any theistic conclusion.

response.rationale: The reply accepts that explanatory superiority cannot erase low priors or contrary total evidence and narrows the claim to some reason for theism.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly contacts the confidence objection and gives the qualified consequence, while not resolving the underlying candidacy dispute.

precisionFindings.rationale: The distinction between local moral evidence and an all-things-considered conclusion is express and stable.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speaker deliberately claims only some reason for belief and acknowledges that total evidence could still favor atheism.

charity.alternative: The candidacy and secular-explanation objections may defeat the argument rather than merely reduce its confidence.
charity.decisiveQualification: The reply narrows the conclusion but does not itself establish that the moral evidence has positive likelihood value.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The conclusion is coherently bounded by priors and total evidence, with only the positive evidential bridge left implicit.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The qualification is philosophically well motivated, but the move does not independently demonstrate the claimed comparative superiority.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central burden requiring a bounded conclusion after priors, rivals, and total evidence are considered.

representationalCharity.rationale: It fairly accommodates the objections' force while leaving their deeper evidential challenge unresolved.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt expressly calls the conclusion epistemically modest, claims only some reason for God, and allows that the total evidence may still favor atheism.

moves.speaker: David Baggett
moves.proposition: The relevant transformation question is not whether ordinary moral improvement occurs, but whether secular naturalism can sustain realistic hope for complete moral transformation.
moves.attributionBasis: Baggett announces a final point about moral transformation and distinguishes total transformation from ordinary improvement within one continuous turn.

response.rationale: The constructive move distinguishes ordinary improvement from realistic hope for total moral transformation and asks whether secular naturalism can sustain the latter.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It sharply defines a stronger transformation explanandum, though it gives little argument that this aspiration is evidentially mandatory.

precisionFindings.rationale: The contrast with ordinary improvement is explicit, but 'total moral transformation' lacks a detailed success condition.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move poses a comparative challenge and explicitly concedes secular ordinary improvement rather than claiming demonstrated impossibility.

charity.alternative: Secular accounts need explain attainable moral improvement, not guarantee complete perfection beyond mortal life.
charity.decisiveQualification: The affirmative must justify why realistic hope for complete transformation is itself a genuine datum requiring explanation.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinction is coherent, but the inference from moral aspiration to an explanatory burden remains an important compressed bridge.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move offers a conceptual distinction and concession but little evidence that total transformation is realistic, universal, or explanatorily required.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It strongly supports the subsidiary transformation bridge by defining the distinctive horizon attributed to theism.

representationalCharity.rationale: The concession to ordinary improvement is fair, but the move does not fully defend the stronger target against the secular alternative.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt explicitly concedes moral improvement in this world and contrasts it with realistic hope for total transformation under naturalism.

moves.speaker: David Baggett
moves.proposition: Objective moral values are intrinsically good, whereas objective moral duties are binding and authoritative prescriptions that can impose categorical requirements without exception.
moves.attributionBasis: Baggett explicitly introduces what he means by objective moral values and duties and supplies separate definitions and an example.

response.rationale: The move constructively distinguishes intrinsically good values from binding, prescriptive, authoritative duties and identifies some duties as exceptionless categorical requirements.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It clearly fixes the principal ontological terms required for the authority dispute, though it does not yet ground them.

precisionFindings.rationale: Values, duties, authority, and the 'at least sometimes' categorical scope qualification are explicitly differentiated.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move is stipulating the terms of its argument and appropriately limits categorical force to at least some duties.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The conceptual distinctions are explicit, consistent, and suitably qualified, though definition alone does not establish instantiation.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move successfully supports terminological clarity, but it supplies little independent evidence that exceptionless categorical duties exist.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It centrally advances the explananda burden by specifying the objective values and authoritative duties requiring explanation.

representationalCharity.rationale: This is a constructive definition and does not materially represent an opposing position.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt defines objective value as intrinsic moral goodness and duties as binding, prescriptive, authoritative obligations, sometimes categorical.

moves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
moves.proposition: Culturally variable guilt cannot ground objective morality, while actions can still be assessed objectively by their effects on adopted goals such as survival and well-being.
moves.attributionBasis: Dillahunty explicitly disputes Baggett's evidential appeal to guilt and contrasts it with his own goal-relative account of objective assessment.

components.text: The affirmative must show that variable guilt tracks objective authoritative duties rather than culture while distinguishing objectivity from goal-relative assessment.
The proposed moral explananda must be specified independently of disputed definitions of objective morality.

response.rationale: The reply challenges guilt as an objective guide and offers objective consequence assessment relative to well-being, though it does not fully answer categorical authority.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the objectivity dispute and supplies an alternative assessment model, but leaves the categorical-duty component substantially unanswered.

precisionFindings.rationale: Goal-relative objective facts are intelligible, but 'objective morality' and the ill-defined scope of well-being remain partly unstable.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move acknowledges definitional dependence and the breadth of well-being while making a bounded means-end claim.

charity.alternative: Guilt is offered as defeasible evidence of authority, not as a complete foundation or infallible detector of objective morality.
charity.decisiveQualification: Cultural variation weakens guilt's reliability but does not by itself show that no guilt experience tracks genuine wrongdoing.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinction between subjective goals and objective facts about consequences is coherent, but it does not resolve categorical normativity.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Cultural variability and consequence assessment provide relevant support, though no representative evidence or full account of well-being is developed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It strongly supports the subsidiary variable-phenomenology bridge while also bearing on the broader secular account.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply addresses the evidential use of guilt but tends to press variation beyond what the qualified affirmative claim requires.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt stresses definitional dependence, calls well-being broad and ill-defined, and claims objective facts about consequences can be assessed without subjective opinions.

moves.speaker: David Baggett
moves.proposition: The phenomenology of guilt can provide evidence of genuine wrongdoing and moral authority rather than being exhausted by an account in terms of cultural conditioning.
moves.attributionBasis: Baggett recalls and qualifies his earlier use of guilt, then gives a sustained response distinguishing socialization from an experience of objective wrongdoing.

components.text: The variability objection must allow that guilt can remain defeasible evidence of genuine wrongdoing without serving as the entire foundation.

response.rationale: The reply narrows guilt to potential evidence and denies that cultural conditioning exhausts its phenomenology, but offers mainly introspective support.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It directly contacts the variation objection through a qualified evidential claim, without explaining how reliable cases are distinguished.

precisionFindings.rationale: The move expressly limits guilt to potential evidence and disclaims making the whole argument depend on it.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Its cautious evidential force fits the personal phenomenological basis and acknowledges the limited role assigned to guilt.

charity.alternative: Guilt can be culturally produced and highly variable even when it feels authoritative to the subject.
charity.decisiveQualification: The reply only denies that cultural imposition exhausts every experience; it does not claim phenomenology alone proves objective authority.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The qualified inference is coherent, but the bridge from authoritative seeming to genuine moral authority remains materially underdeveloped.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Personal introspection supports the phenomenological report, while reliability and alternatives are not independently tested.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the subsidiary categorical-authority and access bridge through moral phenomenology.

representationalCharity.rationale: It preserves the secular alternative and responds with a suitably narrow, defeasible claim.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt calls guilt potential evidence, disclaims resting the whole argument on it, and reports that its phenomenology does not seem merely culturally imposed.

moves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
moves.proposition: Empathy, universalization, and role reversal can explain conscience and much apparent moral authority without religious commands or a further supernatural foundation.
moves.attributionBasis: Dillahunty identifies empathy as the foundation of guilt and develops the point through Rawlsian role reversal and revised reciprocal treatment.

components.text: The authoritative phenomenology of guilt requires an account that distinguishes supernatural authority from empathy and learned moral cognition.
An explanation of apparent authority does not by itself establish the binding categorical duties defined by the affirmative.

response.rationale: The reply directly proposes empathy, universalization, and role reversal as sources of conscience, but does not fully derive objective categorical authority.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the decisive explanatory alternative to guilt while leaving the ontological status of categorical duties unresolved.

precisionFindings.rationale: The move consistently distinguishes perceived moral authority from its proposed empathic foundation and claims only substantial explanatory reach.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The source offers empathy as a foundation rather than claiming it demonstrably explains every conscience judgment.

charity.alternative: The affirmative treats guilt as evidence of genuine wrongdoing, not as a product of explicit parental or religious commands alone.
charity.decisiveQualification: An empathic causal account must still explain why the resulting demands appear categorically authoritative and sometimes oppose self-interest.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Empathy, universalization, and role reversal form a coherent psychological account, with the normativity bridge left implicit.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The mechanisms are plausible and specifically identified, but their sufficiency and comparative advantage receive limited empirical support.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It centrally supports the secular moral account of conscience and moral cognition.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move avoids reducing conscience solely to indoctrination but does not fully engage the authority qualification.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt rejects a simple parental, communal, or religious indoctrination story and identifies empathy as the foundational contributor to guilt.

moves.speaker: David Baggett
moves.proposition: Exceptionally obvious foundational moral principles can be rationally accepted as properly basic axioms from which further ethical reasoning proceeds without inferential proof.
moves.attributionBasis: Baggett explicitly frames the difficulty as one concerning ethical first principles and explains their axiomatic or properly basic epistemic status.

components.text: The demand for an inferential proof of every foundational moral truth should be replaced by assessment of whether some principles are properly basic.
Variable guilt does not determine whether exceptionally obvious moral principles can be rationally basic.

response.rationale: The reply justifies treating exceptionally obvious principles as axiomatic starting points when no more evident premise is available, preserving the knowledge issue.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It directly reframes the justificatory demand and states the epistemic consequence, though it offers no reliability discriminator.

precisionFindings.rationale: The claim is expressly restricted to exceptionally obvious foundational principles and further reasoning from them.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speaker presents openness to properly basic status and acknowledges difficulty producing a more obvious supporting premise.

charity.alternative: Empathy and shared human cognition may causally explain why principles seem obvious without validating their truth.
charity.decisiveQualification: Proper basicality can confer prima facie rationality but does not by itself establish reliability or a theistic source.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The foundationalist structure is coherent, though the criterion separating genuinely basic insight from powerful prejudice remains compressed.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Extreme obviousness supports prima facie acceptance, but disagreement, defeaters, and reliability receive little supporting analysis.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It strongly advances the subsidiary access bridge by explaining how moral knowledge may be noninferential.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reframe fairly addresses inferential justification while leaving the causal and reliability alternatives open.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt says nothing more obvious can be offered and proposes exceedingly obvious moral principles as properly basic axiomatic starting points.

moves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
moves.proposition: Human-benefiting axioms can generate coherent ethical systems and could arise under godless physical conditions because creatures with shared needs have reasons to converge on them.
moves.attributionBasis: Dillahunty explicitly responds to the discussion of foundational axioms and develops both their practical derivation and naturalistic dependence on creaturely interests.

components.text: Axiomatic moral starting points require an account of why shared physical creatures could converge on them without divine disclosure.
Shared human needs provide an alternative source for convergent moral attitudes and associated conscience.

response.rationale: The reply accepts axiomatic starting points and supplies shared needs and physical conditions as a secular convergence account, though 'randomly plucking' weakens justification.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It directly contacts the foundational-axiom issue and offers a secular origin, but does not establish truth or categorical force.

precisionFindings.rationale: The examples are clear, but the relation between random selection, human benefit, convergence, and moral truth is not fully stable.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The claim is framed as what creatures could construct or converge upon, matching the limited warrant supplied.

charity.alternative: Properly basic principles are claimed as rationally apparent truths, not merely arbitrary axioms selected to construct a useful system.
charity.decisiveQualification: A secular convergence story must address epistemic warrant and categorical authority, not only systemic coherence.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Shared needs can explain convergence on useful axioms, but coherent construction does not entail objective truth or categorical obligation.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Concrete examples illustrate plausible convergence, yet the move supplies little evidence of universality, independence, or justificatory force.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It materially supports the central secular account of moral reasoning and convergence.

representationalCharity.rationale: The response engages axioms but materially weakens the affirmative alternative by treating them as tentatively plucked assumptions.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt describes tentatively accepting axioms such as life over death, health over sickness, and pleasure over pain to create a moral system.

moves.speaker: David Baggett
moves.proposition: Some moral obligations are categorical requirements and therefore cannot be reduced to instrumental reasoning about how to achieve goals that an agent has already chosen.
moves.attributionBasis: The uninterrupted turn continues Baggett's comparison of the two moral systems and presents his categorical-obligation example.

components.text: A system built from adopted axioms must explain categorical obligations rather than only instrumental reasoning toward chosen ends.
Empathic motivation does not by itself establish that moral requirements bind regardless of an agent's goals.

response.rationale: The reply expressly diagnoses the secular construction as instrumental and states the defeating consequence that at least some obligations purport to be categorical.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It directly identifies the inference's central limitation, though it does not independently prove that categorical obligations exist.

precisionFindings.rationale: Instrumental and categorical oughts are clearly contrasted, and the claim is limited to at least some moral obligations.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speaker says he is inclined to suggest the distinction and restricts the conclusion rather than claiming universal categorical force.

charity.alternative: The secular view can objectively assess means after adopting foundational values and need not claim agents choose every end arbitrarily.
charity.decisiveQualification: Even objective means-end facts do not alone show why an agent who rejects the end is categorically bound.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinction yields a strong undercutting inference, with the existence and source of categorical duties remaining separate burdens.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The phenomenological distinction is recognizable and carefully limited, but no independent cases or argument establish irreducible categoricity.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It centrally attacks the secular no-grounding-need bridge by identifying what instrumental assessment leaves unexplained.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply grants the legitimacy of practical reasoning and targets its precise residual limitation.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt grants the legitimacy of goal-directed practical reasoning but calls it instrumental and contrasts it with at least some moral obligations.

moves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
moves.proposition: Once concern for well-being is adopted, actions can be evaluated by whether they advance or frustrate that goal without introducing additional categorical oughts.
moves.attributionBasis: The turn explicitly describes Dillahunty's revised treatment of oughts and develops secular answers to Baggett's examples.

components.text: The categorical-duty challenge requires showing why objective assessment relative to adopted well-being needs additional oughts after the initial commitment.
The distinction between categorical and instrumental oughts remains disputed rather than settled by definition.

response.rationale: The reply directly concedes the initial concern for well-being and argues that subsequent judgments are objective means-end assessments without further oughts.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the instrumental-versus-categorical dispute but does not answer why the initial end binds or whether some duties override it.

precisionFindings.rationale: The initial commitment and subsequent goal-relative assessments are explicitly separated, with a clear conditional scope.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The means-end point is strong, but saying there are no further oughts compresses normative standards for selecting acts and resolving conflicts.

charity.alternative: The affirmative agrees that instrumental reasoning is legitimate but claims some obligations bind independently of an adopted goal.
charity.decisiveQualification: The reply explains assessment conditional on well-being, not the alleged categorical authority or the rational necessity of that end.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The conditional means-end structure is coherent, though the assertion that no oughts remain overlooks standards embedded in measurement and tradeoffs.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The conceptual account is plausible and explicit but lacks support for well-being's adequacy across conflicts, persons, and categorical cases.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central claim that objective moral assessment can proceed without additional divine categorical grounding.

representationalCharity.rationale: It recognizes the two kinds of ought and candidly concedes that the affirmative example is more difficult.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt concedes an initial ought of caring about well-being, then describes evaluating whether actions move toward or away from that goal.

moves.speaker: David Baggett
moves.proposition: An account restricted to human flourishing is morally too narrow because animal suffering and the formation of a person's moral character can also matter intrinsically.
moves.attributionBasis: Following the moderator's transition, Baggett resumes the exchange, addresses the animal example, and connects it to moral transformation.

components.text: A well-being or human-flourishing standard must explain moral concern for nonhuman suffering and the agent's character.
Human-benefiting axioms may be too narrow to cover intrinsically significant nonhuman cases.

response.rationale: The reply contacts the scope of the secular end with an animal-torture counterexample and suggests that character matters beyond human flourishing narrowly construed.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It directly identifies a material coverage gap, though broader sentient well-being could absorb much of the challenge.

precisionFindings.rationale: The animal example is clear, but 'human flourishing' may denote either exclusively human benefit or a broader flourishing ethic.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move presents a challenge and says the account may be too constricting rather than claiming decisive refutation.

charity.alternative: A well-being framework can include animal welfare and the effects of cruelty on human character rather than restricting value to immediate human benefit.
charity.decisiveQualification: If those expansions are allowed, the example tests specification and scope more than the viability of the framework itself.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The counterexample coherently pressures a human-exclusive scope, but it is not decisive against broader sentient or character-inclusive flourishing.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The cat-torture case is a specific intuitive test, though no argument establishes that broader well-being cannot accommodate it.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It centrally attacks the adequacy and breadth of the secular moral account.

representationalCharity.rationale: The challenge is live but underdevelops the strongest inclusive interpretation of well-being.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt asks how human flourishing extends to animal rights and uses torturing a cat or bobcat as an apparently wrong act outside a narrow scope.

moves.speaker: David Baggett
moves.proposition: Binding, objective, prescriptive moral obligations call for explanation, and a loving creator who enables moral apprehension offers an account of their authority.
moves.attributionBasis: Baggett gives a sustained first-person exposition of his abductive moral argument and contrasts it with Dillahunty's account throughout the turn.

components.text: The conditional well-being account must explain genuinely binding, objective, prescriptive authority rather than only direction toward an adopted goal.
Constructed axioms must account for moral authority rather than merely generating a coherent system.

response.rationale: The reply returns to the alleged authoritative explanandum and proposes a loving creator as an explanation, but the creator-to-authority bridge is asserted more than defended.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the decisive authority gap and offers the theistic account, though comparative superiority remains underdeveloped.

precisionFindings.rationale: The authority claim and loving-creator proposal are recoverable, but their dependence on the reality of categorical authority is only implicitly conditional.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The account is offered as explanatory, but the excerpt does not sufficiently compare alternatives or derive authority from loving creation.

charity.alternative: The secular account denies that any authority beyond objective means-end assessment needs explanation.
charity.decisiveQualification: The theistic proposal gains purchase only if irreducibly categorical authority has first been established rather than stipulated.

logicalCoherence.rationale: A loving creator can coherently be proposed as a personal authority, but creation and love do not by themselves entail every binding prescription.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move specifies the phenomenon and candidate, yet supplies limited defense of the grounding relation or comparative advantage over secular accounts.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly advances the central affirmative comparative-advantage bridge concerning moral authority.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply acknowledges the secular denial but does not fully discharge the antecedent burden.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt focuses on binding, objective, prescriptive, authoritative obligation, asks what explains it, and contrasts the proposed account with denial of real authority.

moves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
moves.proposition: Methodological naturalism permits demonstrated supernatural causes but rejects an unexplained deity that adds mystery without predictive or explanatory power.
moves.attributionBasis: Dillahunty corrects Baggett's characterization of his position and then presents a continuous methodological and explanatory critique.

components.text: The loving-creator hypothesis must be demonstrable and add predictive or explanatory content rather than merely naming a further mystery.
Candidate explanations must satisfy methodological standards rather than receiving automatic admission because they are metaphysically possible.

response.rationale: The reply directly challenges divine candidacy under methodological naturalism and allows supernatural causes in principle if demonstrated.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the decisive methodological and explanatory demand, though its demonstration standard is not fully reconciled with abduction.

precisionFindings.rationale: Philosophical and methodological naturalism are distinguished, and supernatural explanation is explicitly conditionally admissible.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The methodological distinction is well stated, but requiring demonstration may be stronger than ordinary abductive confirmation.

charity.alternative: The affirmative offers theism as an abductive explanatory candidate, not as an unexplained label or deductively demonstrated cause.
charity.decisiveQualification: The candidate still needs discriminating explanatory content and evidential access sufficient for comparison.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinction and conditional openness are coherent, though 'demonstrable' risks imposing a stronger standard than the comparative method requires.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The methodological principle is clearly articulated, but the claim that God adds only mystery or lacks predictions receives limited case-specific support.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It centrally supports the theistic-liabilities bridge by attacking admissibility and explanatory content.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move admits supernatural explanation in principle but somewhat raises the opposing claim from comparative support to demonstration.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt distinguishes philosophical from methodological naturalism and says supernatural explanations are permitted once demonstrable rather than merely appealed to.

moves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
moves.proposition: Positing God as morality's foundation does not resolve moral disagreement unless people can reliably identify the good deity and access that deity's requirements.
moves.attributionBasis: Dillahunty explicitly introduces a major stumbling block and develops it through historical disagreement and a good-deity identification challenge.

components.text: A divine authority account must explain how people identify the morally perfect deity and reliably access that deity's requirements amid disagreement.
Claims of immediate moral knowledge require a way to handle severe disagreement and confident religious error.

response.rationale: The reply directly presses identification and access, using historical religious disagreement to show that positing a divine foundation does not resolve moral disputes.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly contacts the account's decisive epistemic liability and states the consequence for explanatory usefulness.

precisionFindings.rationale: The identification, access, disagreement, and resolution demands are explicit and consistently scoped to the account's epistemic payoff.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The historical example supports a strong access problem without claiming that disagreement logically disproves divine grounding.

charity.alternative: Theism may ground moral truth even if human beings imperfectly identify God or misunderstand divine requirements.
charity.decisiveQualification: Imperfect access does not refute ontology, but it weakens an explanatory advantage concerning moral knowledge and practical resolution.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference from persistent access failures to reduced epistemic explanatory advantage is explicit and appropriately limited.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The Nazi example and broader historical disagreement are concrete, though one notorious case cannot establish the full frequency or comparative rate.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly advances the central theistic-liabilities bridge through divine identification and access.

representationalCharity.rationale: The objection accurately targets epistemic payoff rather than treating disagreement as a direct disproof of God.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt asks what the classical-theist foundation achieves without access, cites conflicting historical claims of divine support, and asks how disputes are resolved.

moves.speaker: David Baggett
moves.proposition: Theistic ethics requires a morally perfect, maximally great God rather than an arbitrary deity, and moral considerations can help distinguish that hypothesis from finite or capricious gods.
moves.attributionBasis: Baggett accepts the relevance of Dillahunty's questions and answers by restricting the divine hypothesis and contrasting classes of deity.

components.text: The identification objection requires specifying which conception of God can ground ethics and how moral considerations narrow the candidate field.
A theistic candidate requires discriminating properties rather than an unrestricted appeal to supernatural agency.

response.rationale: The reply denies that every deity qualifies and specifies a maximally great, omni-property candidate, but only sketches how moral evidence identifies it.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts candidate specification but leaves reliable access to requirements and independent identification substantially unanswered.

precisionFindings.rationale: The maximally great candidate is clear, but the exact omni-properties and moral criteria doing the narrowing are not fully specified.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speaker says moral considerations can narrow the field, while the excerpt supplies only a preliminary sketch of that discrimination.

charity.alternative: The access objection concerns not merely arbitrary gods but people's reliable identification of the good deity and its requirements.
charity.decisiveQualification: Specifying a morally perfect candidate does not yet show that humans can identify its existence, nature, or commands without circularity.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Restricting the hypothesis to a morally perfect maximally great being is coherent, though using moral considerations to identify the moral ground risks circularity.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move provides useful specification but little independent evidence that the omni-property candidate is uniquely favored over rivals.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It centrally attacks the divine-identification liability by narrowing and morally specifying the candidate.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply fairly rejects arbitrary deity concepts but only partially addresses the strongest epistemic objection.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt says theistic ethics fails on many God concepts and invokes moral considerations and omni-properties to narrow natural theology's field.

moves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
moves.proposition: Confidence in an abductive conclusion should be proportioned to the quality and depth of the available pool of candidate explanations.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator solicits reactions, and this response matches Dillahunty's earlier stated reservations about abductive reasoning.

components.text: Even a specified theistic candidate warrants confidence only relative to the depth and quality of the whole explanatory candidate pool.
The bounded conclusion must reflect bad-lot risk and limited understanding, not merely acknowledge generic prior probability.

response.rationale: The reply directly imposes a candidate-pool confidence constraint and states that shallow understanding can leave even the best available explanation far from reasonable conclusion.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly contacts comparative confidence and gives the defeating consequence, though it does not inventory omitted candidates.

precisionFindings.rationale: Confidence, candidate-pool quality, disciplinary depth, and the bounded consequence are all explicit.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Proportioning confidence to pool quality is asserted as a methodological requirement while uncertainty is central to the claim.

charity.alternative: The affirmative already limits the conclusion to some reason for theism within total evidence rather than a decisive verdict.
charity.decisiveQualification: That modesty helps, but the positive evidential increment still depends on comparison against a sufficiently representative pool.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The link between incomplete candidate exploration and limited abductive confidence is explicit, consistent, and appropriately conditional.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The cross-domain comparison supports the general methodological point, though the actual candidate pool's depth is not systematically documented.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It maximally supports the subsidiary limited-confidence bridge through the bad-lot constraint.

representationalCharity.rationale: The objection preserves the qualified conclusion and identifies the residual condition it must satisfy.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt says confidence must reflect pool quality, contrasts well- and poorly-understood scientific areas, and warns that a best option may remain inconclusive.

moves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
moves.proposition: Persistent divine hiddenness is morally unexpected if a good creator could clarify a consequential dispute whose prolonged uncertainty causes harm.
moves.attributionBasis: The passage remains within Dillahunty's assigned closing remarks and explicitly identifies its reasoning as a form of the divine-hiddenness argument.

components.text: A maximally good creator must explain why consequential moral and religious uncertainty persists when clarification appears available and harm-reducing.
A loving authority account must address why apparently sufficient natural explanations obscure the alleged divine source.

response.rationale: The reply directly derives an expectation of clearer access from a good creator's moral obligations and identifies hiddenness as a comparative liability.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly contacts the goodness hypothesis and states the moral-expectation consequence, though the no-good-reason premise is compressed.

precisionFindings.rationale: The hiddenness challenge is clear, but the amount of clarification required and the class of harms covered remain underdefined.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The expectation of disclosure is plausible, but 'compounds the moral obligation' assumes limited countervailing relational reasons.

charity.alternative: A good God may have relationship-preserving, freedom-related, or developmental reasons not to make divine reality maximally obvious.
charity.decisiveQualification: Those reasons must explain why less coercive clarification could not reduce serious harm while preserving relational goods.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The expectation from goodness to harm-reducing clarification is coherent, with the exclusion of countervailing reasons left as a material bridge.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Persistent dispute and apparently sufficient natural explanations are concrete considerations, but harm magnitude and feasible divine alternatives are not documented.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly advances the central theistic-liabilities bridge through moral divine hiddenness.

representationalCharity.rationale: The source raises a strong moral expectation but does not fully assess the best relational hiddenness alternative.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt argues that a creator who gave humans inquiry capacities would bear greater responsibility if apparently sufficient natural explanations were misleading.

moves.speaker: David Baggett
moves.proposition: Divine hiddenness may reflect relational priorities beyond producing bare belief in God's existence, because recognizing that someone exists is not equivalent to having a relationship.
moves.attributionBasis: Baggett explicitly turns to the hiddenness issue and develops a relational analogy during his moderator-assigned closing response.

components.text: The hiddenness objection must consider whether God's relational purposes differ from merely producing bare belief in divine existence.
Relational priorities may explain some hiddenness but do not independently supply reliable moral access.

response.rationale: The reply directly supplies a possible relational reason for hiddenness and distinguishes existence-belief from relationship, but does not answer the harm and clarification component.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the decisive possibility of justified hiddenness while leaving the opponent's less-coercive clarification and harm challenge unanswered.

precisionFindings.rationale: The belief-versus-relationship distinction is clear, but 'other priorities' and the appropriate measure of hiddenness remain underspecified.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speaker offers probable or potential reasons rather than claiming to know God's actual reasons, matching the limited analogy.

charity.alternative: The hiddenness objection allows that relationship matters but asks why a good God cannot clarify existence and moral truth without coercing relationship.
charity.decisiveQualification: Bare belief is not relationship, yet reliable awareness is ordinarily a prerequisite for entering a relationship and avoiding harmful error.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinction blocks a simple inference from love to maximal obviousness, but does not show that substantial hiddenness promotes relationship.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The spousal analogy illustrates the distinction, while the claimed divine priorities remain speculative and are not compared with less-hidden alternatives.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It centrally attacks the theistic-liabilities bridge by offering a relational account of hiddenness.

representationalCharity.rationale: The response identifies a relevant distinction but omits the objection's decisive compatibility challenge.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt proposes reasons for a measure of hiddenness, says God may prioritize more than producing belief, and analogizes belief in a spouse's existence to relationship.
